title: Opportunities to Reduce Fish Mortality During Early Life Stages in Reservoir Areas
content:
Abstract

Until recently, reservoir areas have been regarded as death traps for pelagic spawners during their early life stages (drifting eggs and young larvae). This is because previous reservoir ecological operation practices modeled these organisms as particles without motility, and managers therefore believed that a drifting passage with a continuous high-flow-velocity was required for them to safely pass through a reservoir. However, this kind of passage requires a tremendous water release from reservoirs, so it is difficult to implement during real-world reservoir operation. In the present study, we examined whether intermittent vertical movement by young grass carp larvae could reduce the flow velocity required for safe passage through reservoirs. To measure this movement behavior, we conducted an experiment that mimicked reservoir conditions, with water temperature and dissolved oxygen controlled. In addition, we developed a drift model that integrated larval behavior, hydrodynamics, and a particle-tracking approach to simulate mortality rates under different scenarios. We found that active movement of young larvae partially counteracted sinking in reservoirs, and reduced by 20% the flow velocity required to establish a drifting passage, relative to estimates based on the conventional assumption that larvae behave as completely passive particles. These findings reveal opportunities to protect young fish in reservoirs, where such protection was once thought to be unfeasible.
